items.item: A Soda data contract is a YAML document of data quality checks, similar to unit tests for software.

at.step: Reveal: the rest of the landscape, named

items.item: Deequ is a library on Apache Spark for "unit tests for data," measuring data quality in large datasets.

at.step: Reveal: the rest of the landscape, named

items.item: DQX defines and runs data-quality checks in PySpark pipelines and notebooks, for batch and streaming.

at.step: Reveal: the rest of the landscape, named

items.item: Being a gate (running before publish, able to block) and being cheap are two separate properties — the Prove It scenario's full-table gate shows a gate can be exactly as expensive as a post-hoc scan if what it checks is the whole table every single run.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: A dbt data test and a GX expectation computing the same not-null rule on the same data and reaching the same verdict is the direct, run demonstration of this chapter's own thesis for tooling: different engines, one question, same answer when the rule is the same.

at.step: Reveal: an expectation suite

items.item: The GX suite catching a negative amount that none of dbt's four built-in generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) would have caught on their own is why a real team often runs more than one framework rather than picking just one.

at.step: Reveal: an expectation suite

items.item: A data-quality facet attaching a check's result to a dataset node is the same mechanism the lineage topic's own facet system defined generically — this topic's checks are one more kind of fact a lineage event can carry, not a separate reporting channel.

at.topic: OpenLineage: events, facets and lineage graphs
at.quote: facets (schema, column lineage, data quality, SQL)

items.item: The sampled estimate reporting zero on data that actually has a defect is a sharper failure mode than undercounting: a dashboard reading zero defects looks identical whether the data is actually clean or the sample simply never saw the one bad row.

at.step: Reveal: sampling, and what it misses

items.item: GX's own stewardship announcement naming an exact transition date (GX Cloud unavailable after 1 June) is the same kind of dated, checkable fact this chapter has flagged before for Amundsen and for Apache Polaris — stated with its own date rather than assumed current.

Incremental metrics and sampling are the same cost lever Chapter 5's sketches apply to distinct counting and membership, generalised here to a data-quality check: compute less per run, at a stated (and in sampling's case, nonzero) risk of missing something.

at.step: Reveal: incremental metrics

items.item: The predict question's two scenarios (gate-vs-scan placement, then a full-table gate's own growing cost) both test the same underlying claim from different angles: where a check runs and what a check costs are two separate decisions, not one.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Naming Deequ, Soda and DQX without running any of them, while running dbt and GX to completion, is a disclosed scope limit set directly by this environment's own missing dependencies (no Spark, no connected data platform), not an editorial choice about which tools matter more.

at.step: Reveal: the rest of the landscape, named

items.item: A unit test passing on mocked rows while a data test fails on the real built data, in the same lab run, is the clearest possible demonstration that the two check different things: the model's own logic is correct, but the data it was actually fed that run was not.
